title: Neutropenia
subject: Medicine
summary: Neutropenia is a low absolute neutrophil count that raises infection risk. Diagnose with a CBC, stage severity, identify reversible causes, and manage promptly, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Neutropenia is defined by an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 1500/µL on a peripheral blood smear. Severe neutropenia is ANC < 500/µL; profound < 100/µL.
b: Confirm with repeat CBC if patient is stable

t.b: What is the neutrophil count? – Confirms neutropenia and assesses other cytopenias

sections.p: Stage guides infection risk and urgency of intervention.
In East African low‑resource hospitals, think of infections, drugs, and marrow infiltration.
b: HIV infection (especially with opportunistic TB or cryptococcus)
Chemotherapy or anti‑TB drugs (e.g., rifampicin, isoniazid)

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic until infection occurs; look for fever, oral ulcers, skin pustules, or rapid deterioration.
Targeted tests identify reversible causes and assess infection risk.

t.b: Is HIV present? – Positive test prompts ART review and prophylaxis
Is active TB present? – Positive result directs anti‑TB therapy, which may affect marrow
Are there immature cells or dysplasia? – Suggests marrow infiltration or drug effect
Is there a nutritional deficiency? – Low levels guide supplementation

sections.p: Severe neutropenia predisposes to life‑threatening infections.
b: Rapidly expanding cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis
Septic shock signs (hypotension, altered mental status)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect against infection, and consider growth‑factor support when resources allow.
b: Stop offending drugs (e.g., zidovudine) and switch to safer alternatives
Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Pseudomonas for ANC < 500/µL with fever
Give G‑CSF (filgrastim) if available for profound neutropenia or anticipated chemotherapy‑induced drop
Implement strict hand hygiene, protective isolation if possible, and prophylactic cotrimoxazole for HIV‑positive patients

sections.p: Monitor ANC twice weekly until recovery; educate on infection avoidance.
b: Repeat CBC every 3‑5 days in severe cases
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza when counts recover
Counsel on safe herbal use and nutrition

sections.p: Conditions that mimic low neutrophils on routine labs.
b: Leukopenia due to lymphopenia (different infection risk)
Automated counters may misclassify immature cells as lymphocytes, under‑estimating neutropenia
Severe anemia can falsely lower calculated ANC; verify with manual differential

faq.q: Why is neutropenia more dangerous in HIV patients?
faq.a: HIV impairs cell‑mediated immunity; low neutrophils further reduce bacterial defence, raising sepsis risk.
Yes, severe malaria can suppress marrow and cause drug‑induced neutropenia from antimalarials.
For profound neutropenia (<100/µL) with fever, or when chemotherapy is expected to cause a severe drop and supportive care is possible.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever and ANC 400/µL – what is your immediate management? — Start empiric anti‑pseudomonal β‑lactam, assess for source, consider G‑CSF if available.
How does severe neutropenia change your interpretation of a normal chest X‑ray? — Recognise that infection may be present despite a clear film; rely on clinical signs and early cultures.
Which drug commonly used in East Africa can cause neutropenia and should be stopped? — Zidovudine; replace with a less myelotoxic regimen.
What laboratory finding would suggest bone‑marrow infiltration rather than drug effect? — Presence of immature granulocytes >20% of total neutrophils or pancytopenia on CBC.
Why is prophylactic cotrimoxazole recommended in neutropenic HIV patients? — It prevents Pneumocystis jirovecii and bacterial infections, reducing mortality.
A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops neutropenia; what is the next step? — Review for isoniazid or rifampicin toxicity, consider temporary drug hold, and monitor ANC closely.
Explain why a low ANC does not always require G‑CSF in low‑resource settings. — Cost, limited availability, and modest benefit unless ANC <100/µL with infection.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral to a tertiary centre? — Fever with hypotension or rapidly progressing cellulitis despite antibiotics.
